Hypertension is defined as systolic blood pressure of 130 mmHg or higher or diastolic blood pressure of 80 mmHg or higher. Stage 1 hypertension is 130-139/80-89 mmHg; stage 2 is 140/90 mmHg or higher. Accurate diagnosis requires multiple readings on separate occasions, preferably using validated automated devices with proper cuff size. Out-of-office monitoring with ambulatory or home blood pressure measurement is recommended when white-coat or masked hypertension is suspected.

Initial evaluation should assess cardiovascular risk, target-organ damage, and secondary causes. Obtain a thorough history including family history, diet, sodium intake, alcohol use, physical activity, sleep apnea symptoms, and medication use including NSAIDs and decongestants. Physical examination should include bilateral arm pressures, BMI, waist circumference, fundoscopic exam when indicated, cardiovascular and pulmonary examination, abdominal bruits, and peripheral pulses.

Laboratory testing at diagnosis includes serum electrolytes, creatinine, estimated GFR, fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipid profile, urinalysis, and ECG. Additional testing is guided by clinical suspicion for secondary hypertension, such as aldosterone-renin ratio for primary aldosteronism, renal imaging for renovascular disease, or thyroid function when clinically indicated.

Lifestyle modification is foundational for all patients with elevated blood pressure. Recommend weight loss for overweight patients, DASH-style dietary pattern rich in fruits and vegetables with reduced saturated fat, sodium restriction to less than 2300 mg daily (ideally 1500 mg for higher-risk patients), increased dietary potassium unless contraindicated, regular aerobic physical activity at least 150 minutes per week, moderation of alcohol intake, and smoking cessation.

Pharmacologic treatment is indicated for stage 1 hypertension with clinical cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or 10-year ASCVD risk of 10% or greater; and for all patients with stage 2 hypertension. First-line agents include thiazide diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and calcium channel blockers. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are preferred in patients with diabetes or CKD. Black patients without heart failure or CKD may have better outcomes with calcium channel blockers or thiazides as initial therapy.

Combination therapy is often required to achieve blood pressure goals. Single-pill combinations improve adherence. Target blood pressure is generally less than 130/80 mmHg for most adults, individualized for older adults, those with orthostatic symptoms, or significant comorbidity. Reassess blood pressure control every 3-6 months once at goal; monitor electrolytes and renal function within 2-4 weeks after initiating or intensifying ACE inhibitor, ARB, or diuretic therapy.

Resistant hypertension is defined as blood pressure above goal despite three antihypertensive agents at optimal doses including a diuretic. Evaluate for nonadherence, white-coat effect, secondary causes, and interfering substances. Spironolactone is often effective as a fourth-line agent when potassium and renal function permit. Referral to hypertension specialist is appropriate for refractory cases or when secondary hypertension is suspected.

Hypertensive emergencies require immediate blood pressure reduction in a monitored setting with intravenous agents. Hypertensive urgencies without acute target-organ damage should not be treated with rapid lowering; oral agents and close outpatient follow-up are preferred. Patient education should emphasize lifelong therapy, home monitoring technique, medication adherence, and recognition of symptoms requiring urgent care.

The common cold is a viral upper respiratory tract infection most often caused by rhinoviruses. Typical symptoms include nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, sore throat, cough, and mild malaise. Fever is uncommon in adults but may occur in children. Symptoms usually peak around day 2-3 and resolve within 7-10 days, though cough may persist up to 2-3 weeks.

Diagnosis is clinical; testing is not routinely indicated unless influenza or COVID-19 is suspected based on epidemiology or severity. Distinguish from allergic rhinitis (itching, clear discharge, seasonal pattern) and bacterial sinusitis (symptoms beyond 10 days with worsening course, facial pain, purulent discharge).

Treatment is supportive. Rest, adequate hydration, saline nasal irrigation, and honey for cough in adults and children over 1 year may provide symptom relief. Over-the-counter analgesics such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen may reduce discomfort. Intranasal ipratropium may reduce rhinorrhea in adults. Zinc supplementation within 24 hours of symptom onset may modestly shorten duration in some studies but is not routinely recommended due to inconsistent benefit and adverse effects.

Antibiotics are not indicated for uncomplicated viral upper respiratory infections and should be avoided to reduce resistance and adverse drug effects. Decongestants may be used short-term in adults without hypertension, cardiovascular disease, or urinary retention. Return precautions include high fever lasting more than 3 days, severe headache, shortness of breath, chest pain, dehydration, or symptoms worsening after initial improvement.

Acute pharyngitis is most commonly viral, with group A Streptococcus (GAS) responsible for approximately 5-15% of adult cases and 20-30% of pediatric cases depending on age and season. Clinical features suggesting GAS include sudden onset sore throat, fever, tonsillar exudates, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and absence of cough. Centor or McIsaac scores help guide testing and treatment decisions but do not replace clinical judgment.

Rapid antigen detection testing or throat culture is recommended when GAS is suspected before initiating antibiotics. Asymptomatic contacts should not be routinely tested or treated. Antibiotic therapy for confirmed GAS pharyngitis reduces symptom duration modestly, prevents suppurative complications, and decreases transmission. Preferred agents include penicillin V, amoxicillin, or a first-generation cephalosporin in non-allergic patients. Macrolides or clindamycin are alternatives in penicillin allergy.

Supportive care includes analgesics, warm saline gargles, and adequate hydration. Corticosteroids may provide short-term symptom relief in severe exudative pharyngitis but are not routinely required. Patients should be advised to return if symptoms persist beyond 7 days, severe unilateral throat pain develops suggesting peritonsillar abscess, or signs of airway compromise appear.

Type 2 diabetes mellitus is characterized by insulin resistance and progressive beta-cell dysfunction. Diagnosis is established by fasting plasma glucose 126 mg/dL or higher, HbA1c 6.5% or higher, random glucose 200 mg/dL or higher with classic symptoms, or 2-hour post-load glucose 200 mg/dL or higher on oral glucose tolerance testing.

Initial management emphasizes lifestyle intervention including medical nutrition therapy, weight reduction of 5-10% when overweight, regular physical activity, and diabetes self-management education. Assess cardiovascular risk, blood pressure, lipids, renal function, retinopathy screening, and foot examination at diagnosis and regularly thereafter.

Pharmacologic therapy should be individualized. Metformin remains first-line unless contraindicated. In patients with established ASCVD, heart failure, or CKD, agents with proven cardiovascular or renal benefit such as SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists are preferred independent of baseline HbA1c. Insulin is indicated for symptomatic hyperglycemia, catabolic features, or when glycemic targets are not met with other agents.

Glycemic targets are generally HbA1c below 7% for many adults, with less stringent goals for older adults with limited life expectancy or high hypoglycemia risk. Monitor HbA1c every 3-6 months. Hypoglycemia prevention, medication adherence, and screening for complications are essential components of long-term care.

An asthma exacerbation is an acute or subacute worsening of symptoms and lung function from baseline. Triggers include viral respiratory infections, allergen exposure, poor adherence, and environmental irritants. Assess severity by symptoms, respiratory rate, pulse, oxygen saturation, peak expiratory flow or spirometry, and ability to speak in full sentences.

Mild to moderate exacerbations in the outpatient setting are managed with increased inhaled short-acting beta-agonist (SABA) every 4-6 hours as needed, a short course of oral corticosteroids (typically prednisone 40-50 mg daily for 5-7 days), and optimization of controller therapy. Patients should continue or step up inhaled corticosteroids as appropriate. Review inhaler technique and adherence at every visit.

Urgent referral or emergency care is indicated for oxygen saturation below 92%, silent chest, inability to speak phrases, drowsiness, cyanosis, or poor response to initial bronchodilator therapy. After exacerbation resolution, schedule follow-up within 1-2 weeks to reassess control, adjust maintenance therapy, and provide a written asthma action plan including when to increase medications and when to seek emergency care.
